plan: [I have value $39. Assuming other bidders bid their private values (naive/neutral model), if I bid b I win with probability (b/49)^4 and, conditional on winning, expect to pay 0.6b (the 2nd-highest of the other four). Expected payoff ~ (b/49)^4(39 - 0.6b), maximized at b ≥ 4·39/3 = 52, so constrained optimum is at the upper bound. To secure the win and maximize expected profit, bid the maximum feasible common-range amount: $49.]

[Assume a symmetric increasing equilibrium. For a 3rd-price auction with n=5 and uniform values, the symmetric bidding function is linear b(v)=c*v. Solving the first-order condition for a deviation (using the 2nd-highest of 4 opponents) yields c=4/3. Thus optimal bid = (4/3)*v. For v=20, b=26.666..., rounded to the nearest $0.1.]

[Compute symmetric equilibrium for a 3rd-price auction with 5 bidders and uniform values. Solving the first-order condition (assuming increasing bidding rule) yields a linear equilibrium bid β(v) = (4/3)v. With my value $20, the equilibrium bid is (4/3)*20 = $26.666..., rounded to the nearest $0.1.]

[Bid my true value $6. In a third-price auction with independent uniform draws, bidding your value ensures any win will pay at most your bid, so you can't lose when you win. My private value is small relative to the distribution, so wins will be rare but when they occur the third-highest is typically below $6, yielding positive surplus. I will not overbid to avoid the risk of paying more than my value.]

[With 5 bidders and third-price payment, the winner pays the 3rd-highest bid. My value ($11) is low vs. the 0–49 range; chance I'm the highest is (11/50)^4 ≈ 0.23%. Overbidding risks winning while paying a third-highest bid that exceeds $11, creating a loss. To maximize expected payoff (and avoid negative outcomes) I should avoid forcing wins when unlikely to be highest. Bid minimally (0) to prevent costly wins while still capturing the tiny upside if others also bid zero.]
